items.title: A Late Train
items.body: Sarah arrived at the station at eight in the morning. Her train to Manchester was at 8:20, but the board said it was thirty minutes late. She bought a coffee and sat near the window. When the train finally came, she found a seat by the door and read her book for two hours. She reached Manchester just after eleven.

questions.prompt: What time was Sarah's train supposed to leave?
questions.explanation: The text says her train was at 8:20.

questions.prompt: Why did she wait?
questions.explanation: The board said the train was thirty minutes late.

questions.prompt: What did she do on the train?
questions.explanation: She read her book for two hours.

items.title: Breakfast Around the World
items.body: In Japan, breakfast can be rice, fish and soup. In Turkey, it is bread, cheese, olives and tomatoes. In England, many people eat only toast on a normal day, and a big cooked breakfast on holiday. What people eat in the morning is mostly a habit, not a rule.

questions.prompt: What is a typical Turkish breakfast?
questions.explanation: The text lists bread, cheese, olives and tomatoes.

questions.prompt: According to the text, breakfast choices are mostly
questions.explanation: The last line says it is mostly a habit.

items.title: Where Are the Keys?
items.body: Every morning Leo looks for his keys. Usually they are in his coat, but sometimes they are in the kitchen or under a newspaper. Last week he was ten minutes late for work twice. So on Sunday he put a small bowl by the front door. Now the keys go in the bowl, and Leo leaves the house on time.

questions.prompt: How many times was Leo late last week?
questions.explanation: The text says twice.

questions.prompt: What did Leo buy or use to solve the problem?
questions.explanation: He put a small bowl by the front door.

questions.prompt: Where does Leo usually find his keys?
questions.explanation: Usually they are in his coat.

items.title: Taking It Back
items.body: Nina bought a jacket online. It arrived on Friday, but the sleeves were too long. The website said she could return it within thirty days if she kept the label on. She printed the form, put the jacket back in the bag, and took it to the post office on Saturday. The money came back four days later.

questions.prompt: What was wrong with the jacket?
questions.explanation: The sleeves were too long.

questions.prompt: What did Nina have to keep on the jacket?
questions.explanation: The website said to keep the label on.

questions.prompt: When did she get her money back?
questions.explanation: The money came back four days later.

items.title: A Short Walk Every Day
items.body: Doctor Amin tells his patients the same simple thing: walk for twenty minutes a day. It does not have to be fast, and it does not have to be all at once. Ten minutes in the morning and ten after dinner is fine. Many people think exercise means a gym, expensive shoes and a plan. It does not. It means moving, often.

questions.prompt: How long does the doctor suggest walking each day?
questions.explanation: He says twenty minutes a day.

questions.prompt: Does the walk have to be in one go?
questions.explanation: Ten plus ten is fine.

questions.prompt: What does the doctor think exercise really means?
questions.explanation: The last line says it means moving, often.

items.title: The Flat Upstairs
items.body: The family upstairs moved in three weeks ago. They have two small children, and on Saturday mornings there is a lot of noise. At first Priya was annoyed. Then she met the mother on the stairs, who apologised before Priya said anything. Now Priya minds the noise less. It is the same noise; she just knows where it comes from.

questions.prompt: When is the noise worst?
questions.explanation: The text says Saturday mornings.

questions.prompt: Who apologised first?
questions.explanation: The mother apologised before Priya said anything.

questions.prompt: Why does Priya mind less now?
questions.explanation: The noise is the same; knowing the neighbours changed how she feels.

items.title: The New Badge
items.body: On his first day, Samir was given a badge, a laptop and a list of eleven people to meet. He remembered four of the names. At lunch he sat alone because he did not know where anyone else went. On his second day someone asked him to join them, and he learned that most of the team eats in the park when it is dry.

questions.prompt: How many names did Samir remember?
questions.explanation: He remembered four of the eleven.

questions.prompt: Why did he eat alone on the first day?
options: He did not know where people went
questions.explanation: He did not know where anyone else went.

questions.prompt: Where does the team usually eat?
questions.explanation: Most of the team eats in the park when it is dry.

items.title: One Ticket, Two Buses
items.body: In this city one ticket lasts ninety minutes. You can change buses as many times as you like inside that time without paying again. You buy the ticket from a machine at the stop or from the driver, but the driver charges more. Most people buy a book of ten tickets, which is cheaper still.

questions.prompt: How long does one ticket last?
questions.explanation: The text says ninety minutes.

questions.prompt: Which way of buying is most expensive?
questions.explanation: The driver charges more.

questions.prompt: Can you change buses on one ticket?
options: As often as you like within the time
questions.explanation: You can change as many times as you like inside the ninety minutes.

items.title: The First Week
items.body: Daniel started his new job on a Monday. Nobody told him where the kitchen was, so he drank water from a bottle all day. On Tuesday a colleague called Priya showed him around and introduced him to the team. By Friday he had joined two projects and understood roughly half of the words people used in meetings. He went home tired but satisfied.

questions.prompt: How did Daniel feel at the end of the week?
questions.explanation: The last sentence says tired but satisfied.

questions.prompt: Who helped him?
questions.explanation: Priya showed him around on Tuesday.

questions.prompt: What does roughly half mean here?
questions.explanation: Roughly means approximately.

items.title: Phones at the Table
items.body: A small restaurant in Lisbon offers a ten percent discount to anyone who leaves their phone in a box during the meal. The owner started the idea after he noticed families eating in silence, each person looking down. Most customers accept the offer. A few refuse, saying they need to be reachable for work. The owner says the restaurant is louder now, and he likes it.

questions.prompt: What do customers get for leaving their phone?
questions.explanation: The discount is ten percent.

questions.prompt: Why did the owner start this?
questions.explanation: He noticed families eating in silence.

questions.prompt: How does the owner feel about the change?
questions.explanation: He says he likes that it is louder.

items.title: Back to Class at Forty
items.body: Ravi had not sat an exam for twenty-two years when he enrolled in an evening accounting course. The first month was humiliating: he was slower than the twenty-year-olds and had forgotten how to take notes. By the third month he was faster than most of them, because he had spent two decades doing the work the textbook described. What he had lacked was not the knowledge but the vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Why was the first month hard?
options: He was slower and had forgotten how to study
questions.explanation: He was slower than the younger students and had forgotten how to take notes.

questions.prompt: Why did he improve so quickly?
options: He had real experience of the work
questions.explanation: He had spent two decades doing the work the textbook described.

questions.prompt: What had Ravi actually been missing?
questions.explanation: The last sentence says it was the vocabulary, not the knowledge.

items.title: Why the Bakery Closed
items.body: The bakery on Mill Street had customers every day for nineteen years and still shut last spring. The rent had doubled, flour had gone up by a third, and the owner could not raise prices past what the street would pay. Being busy and being profitable turned out to be two different things, and only one of them keeps the lights on.

questions.prompt: Did the bakery lack customers?
questions.explanation: It had customers every day for nineteen years.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT given as a reason?
questions.explanation: Customers kept coming; the costs were the problem.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the last sentence?
options: Being busy is not the same as making money
questions.explanation: It contrasts being busy with being profitable.

items.title: Ten Cents a Bottle
items.body: When the deposit scheme started, shoppers paid ten cents extra on every bottle and got it back when they returned the empty. Critics said nobody would bother for ten cents. Within a year, nine out of ten bottles were coming back. The people returning them were often not the people who had bought them, which is a second result the designers had not planned for but do not regret.

questions.prompt: What happens when you return the empty bottle?
questions.explanation: The deposit is returned.

questions.prompt: What did critics predict?
options: The scheme would be too expensive
Nobody would bother for ten cents
questions.explanation: Critics said nobody would bother.

questions.prompt: What was the unplanned result?
options: People other than the buyers returned them
questions.explanation: Returners were often not the original buyers.

items.title: Two Time Zones
items.body: For eight months Lena and Kofi were five and a half hours apart. They stopped trying to talk every day, which had felt like an obligation, and picked two long calls a week instead. The calls got better. What surprised them was how much they had to explain: living apart meant no shared small events, so every story needed context before it could be told.

questions.prompt: How far apart were their time zones?
questions.explanation: Five and a half hours.

questions.prompt: What did they change?
options: They switched to two long calls a week
questions.explanation: They picked two long calls a week.

questions.prompt: What surprised them?
options: How much context every story needed
How little they had to say
questions.explanation: Living apart meant every story needed explaining first.

items.title: Volunteers Wanted
items.body: The gate agent announced that the flight was overbooked and asked for volunteers to take the next one, six hours later, in exchange for a voucher. Nobody moved. She raised the offer twice. On the third offer four people stood up at once, and two of them looked annoyed that they had not waited longer. The airline had, in effect, run an auction without calling it one.

questions.prompt: What was the problem with the flight?
questions.explanation: The gate agent said it was overbooked.

questions.prompt: How many times did she raise the offer?
questions.explanation: She raised it twice, and the third offer was accepted.

questions.prompt: Why were two volunteers annoyed?
options: They thought the offer might have gone higher
questions.explanation: They regretted not waiting for a better offer.

items.title: The Password Rule
items.body: For years, office systems demanded a capital, a number and a symbol, and a change every ninety days. The result was predictable: people picked Summer2019! and then Summer2020!, and wrote them on a sticky note. Security teams now advise a long phrase you can remember and almost never change it. The old rule protected the system from a computer guessing, and handed it to anyone with eyes.

questions.prompt: What did the old rule require?
options: A capital, number and symbol every ninety days
questions.explanation: That was the old requirement.

questions.prompt: What do security teams advise now?
options: A long memorable phrase, rarely changed
questions.explanation: A long phrase you can remember.

questions.prompt: What is the criticism of the old rule?
options: It was too weak against computers
It made passwords visible to people
questions.explanation: It defended against guessing but encouraged sticky notes.

items.title: Standing in Line
items.body: A queue is a small contract. Everyone gives up the chance to push forward in return for a guarantee that nobody else will either. It works because breaking it is visible, and because the cost of enforcing it is spread across everyone waiting. Systems that take a ticket and call a number remove the visibility, which is why they need a machine to hold the order that a line held for free.

questions.prompt: What does the writer compare a queue to?
questions.explanation: A queue is called a small contract.

questions.prompt: Why does a queue work, according to the text?
questions.explanation: Breaking it is visible and enforcement is shared.

questions.prompt: What is the drawback of ticket systems?
options: They remove the visibility a line provided
questions.explanation: Removing visibility means a machine must hold the order instead.

items.title: The Quiet Leak
items.body: Ines went through her bank statement line by line for the first time in two years. She found four subscriptions she had forgotten: a music service she had replaced, a cloud plan for photos she had moved, a magazine and a gym she stopped attending in March. Together they came to more than her electricity bill. Cancelling took eleven minutes.

questions.prompt: How many forgotten subscriptions did she find?
questions.explanation: She found four.

questions.prompt: What were they worth together?
options: About the same as her rent
questions.explanation: Together they came to more than her electricity bill.

questions.prompt: What point is the last sentence making?
options: The cost of not checking was far larger than the effort of fixing it
questions.explanation: Eleven minutes against years of payments.

items.title: The Cost of Convenience
items.body: Delivery apps promised to give people back their evenings. In many cities they have, but the convenience is not evenly shared. Riders absorb the traffic, the weather and the pressure of a countdown timer, while restaurants hand over a share of a margin that was already thin. Customers, meanwhile, grow used to a price that does not include any of this. Economists call it an externality; riders call it Tuesday.

questions.prompt: What is the main argument of the text?
options: The convenience has hidden costs carried by others
questions.explanation: The passage lists costs absorbed by riders and restaurants.

questions.prompt: What does thin margin mean?
questions.explanation: A thin margin is a small profit.

questions.prompt: The last sentence is an example of
questions.explanation: Contrasting economists with riders creates irony.

items.title: The Office With No Walls
items.body: Open-plan offices were sold on collaboration and bought on cost per square metre. The research since has been unkind: face-to-face conversation falls when walls come down, and written messages rise to replace it, because people who can be overheard say less. None of this means the walls are coming back. It means the stated reason and the actual reason were never the same reason, and only one of them was ever going to be tested.

questions.prompt: What were open-plan offices publicly justified by?
questions.explanation: They were sold on collaboration.

questions.prompt: What does the research suggest happens?
options: Less face-to-face talk, more written messages
questions.explanation: Conversation falls and written messages rise.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's final point?
options: The real motive was cost, and it was never the claim under test
questions.explanation: The stated reason and the actual reason differed.

items.title: The Result That Would Not Repeat
items.body: A finding is not a fact until someone else can produce it. For a long stretch, journals rewarded novelty and nothing else, so nobody was paid to check. When large replication projects finally ran, a substantial share of celebrated results would not reappear. The uncomfortable part is not that scientists were dishonest - overwhelmingly they were not - but that a system optimising for surprise will reliably produce surprises, whether or not they are true.

questions.prompt: Why did nobody check results for a long time?
questions.explanation: Novelty was the only thing rewarded.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about scientists' honesty?
questions.explanation: The text explicitly says overwhelmingly they were not.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's actual criticism?
options: The incentive system produces surprises regardless of truth
questions.explanation: A system optimising for surprise will produce surprises.

items.title: The Number You Say First
items.body: Conventional advice warns against naming a figure first, on the grounds that you may undershoot. The evidence points the other way in most settings: the first credible number sets the range the rest of the conversation moves within, and the party who sets it usually does better. The caveat is credible. An anchor that the other side dismisses out of hand is not an anchor; it is an insult with a decimal point.

questions.prompt: What is the conventional advice?
questions.explanation: Conventional advice warns against going first.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence suggest?
questions.explanation: The first credible number sets the range and its setter usually does better.

questions.prompt: What does the final sentence add?
questions.explanation: An anchor the other side dismisses does not function as an anchor.

items.title: What Gets Lost
items.body: Translators talk about untranslatable words as though the difficulty were in the vocabulary. Usually it is not. A word like the Portuguese saudade can be explained in a sentence; what cannot be carried across is the fact that speakers reach for it without effort, and that reaching for it is itself part of the meaning. You can translate the definition. You cannot translate the reflex.

questions.prompt: Where does the writer say the difficulty usually lies?
options: In the reflex of reaching for the word
questions.explanation: The definition translates; the effortless reach does not.

questions.prompt: Can saudade be explained?
questions.explanation: The text says it can be explained in a sentence.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's view of the term untranslatable?
options: Misleading about where the problem is
questions.explanation: The writer says the difficulty is usually not the vocabulary.

items.title: Paying Someone Else to Stop
items.body: Carbon offsets let an emitter fund a reduction somewhere cheaper than their own operations. In principle the atmosphere does not care where a tonne is avoided. In practice the scheme rests on a counterfactual - what would have happened anyway - and counterfactuals cannot be audited, only argued. Investigations have repeatedly found forests sold as saved that were never under threat. The instrument is not inherently fraudulent; it is inherently unverifiable, which in a market is close enough to the same thing.

questions.prompt: What is the principle behind offsets?
options: Location of the reduction does not matter to the atmosphere
questions.explanation: A tonne avoided anywhere counts the same.

questions.prompt: What is the practical problem the writer identifies?
questions.explanation: What would have happened anyway can only be argued.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's conclusion?
options: Offsets are unverifiable, which in a market amounts to much the same
questions.explanation: Not inherently fraudulent, but inherently unverifiable.

items.title: Interruption as a Business Model
items.body: The products competing hardest for your attention are free, and this is not a coincidence. Where the user does not pay, the metric that survives is time spent, and the fastest route to time spent is not satisfaction but incompletion - the feed that never ends, the notification that resolves into another. A paid product that wasted your evening would lose a customer. A free one has just had a good quarter.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer say free products fight hardest for attention?
options: Time spent is the metric that survives when nobody pays
questions.explanation: Without payment, time spent becomes the measure.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say drives time spent?
questions.explanation: The fastest route is incompletion, not satisfaction.

questions.prompt: What is the contrast in the final two sentences?
options: Paid products lose customers for wasting time; free ones profit from it
questions.explanation: The same outcome is a loss for one model and a win for the other.

items.title: The Cost of Being the Only One Who Knows
items.body: Every team has a person who is the only one who understands a particular system. It feels like security to be that person and it looks like efficiency to the manager, because the work gets done quickly and no time is spent explaining. The bill arrives later and lands on someone else: the holiday that cannot be taken, the decision that waits a week, the rewrite that follows the resignation. Irreplaceability is a debt the team pays and the individual holds.

questions.prompt: Why does the arrangement look efficient at first?
options: Work is fast and no time goes on explaining
questions.explanation: It is quick and nothing is spent on explanation.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT listed as a later cost?
questions.explanation: Salaries are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: What does the final sentence claim?
options: The team pays a debt the individual holds
questions.explanation: It is a debt the team pays and the individual holds.
